lines.text: The middle size on the menu is often a trap.
Picture a movie theater with two sizes of popcorn.
Small for three dollars. Large for seven.
Most people buy the small. Seven feels like too much.
Now the theater adds a medium, for six dollars and fifty cents.
Almost nobody buys it. It was never meant to sell.
But next to it, the large suddenly looks like a bargain.
Only fifty cents more for a much bigger bucket.
So people switch to the large, and the theater wins.
Researchers call this the decoy effect.
Your brain is bad at judging a price on its own.
So it compares, and the decoy gives it something easy to beat.
You see it with coffee sizes, phone plans and streaming subscriptions.
Often one option is there just to make another look smart.
Here is how to beat it.
Cover the middle option, and look at the other two on their own.
Then decide as if the decoy were never there.
Most of the time, the small was all you wanted.
Follow for more money tricks they use on you every day.

caption: The decoy effect explained: why the medium popcorn makes the large look like a deal, and how to stop overpaying.

lines.text: Milk sits at the back of the store on purpose.
Milk is one of the things people buy most often.
So where does the store put it?
As far from the door as possible.
The official reason is boring, and partly true.
Milk arrives by refrigerated truck at the back dock.
The big walk in coolers sit right behind that wall, so stocking is easy.
But there is a bonus the store never complains about.
To reach the milk, you walk past snacks, sales and shiny displays.
Every extra step is another chance to grab something you did not plan.
When public radio economists dug into it, their answer was both.
Logistics put the milk there. Marketing is happy it stayed.
Here is how to win that walk.
Write a list before you go, and read it at the door.
Take the outer aisle straight to the back, and look only at your list.
Grab your milk, then walk out the same way.
The fastest trip is the cheapest trip.
Follow for the tricks hiding in plain sight.

caption: Why grocery stores put the milk at the back, the logistics and the marketing reason, and how to shop without the expensive walk.

lines.text: The slot machine celebrates while you lose money.
Modern slots let you bet on many lines at once.
Say you bet one dollar across twenty lines.
One line hits and pays back forty cents.
You just lost sixty cents.
But the machine flashes lights, plays a happy tune and counts up your prize.
Researchers call this a loss disguised as a win.
In a study at the University of Waterloo, they measured players' sweat response.
Their bodies reacted to these fake wins just like real ones.
The brain hears the celebration, not the math.
And a later study found the sounds made the effect even stronger.
So a session can feel full of wins while your balance quietly drains.
Here is how to see through it.
Ignore the lights and look only at the number you started with.
If it is lower, every song you heard was a loss.
Better yet, turn the sound off, and the magic disappears.
The house does not need you to win. It needs you to feel like winning.
Follow before the next machine plays you a song.

caption: Losses disguised as wins: how slot machines celebrate when you lose money, what a Waterloo study found, and how to see through it.

lines.text: People bid twice as much when paying by card.
Two professors at MIT ran a real auction for basketball tickets.
Boston Celtics seats, sold to the highest bidder.
Half the bidders were told they would pay with cash.
The other half were told they would pay by credit card.
Same tickets. Same game. Only the payment changed.
The card group's average bid was about twice as high.
A card turns money into a promise you deal with later.
One likely reason is what psychologists call the pain of paying.
Handing over cash hurts a little, and that small hurt slows you down.
Tap to pay and phone wallets take away even more of it.
Every second they remove from checkout removes a little hesitation.
You can put the sting back.
Use cash for the categories where you overspend, like eating out.
Or check your banking app right after every card payment.
Seeing the balance drop brings back the feeling cash gives you.
Money you can feel is money you keep.
Follow so your money stops feeling like a game.

caption: Why paying by card makes you spend more: the MIT ticket auction where card bids were about twice as high, and how to feel your money again.

lines.text: Some sale timers reset every time you reload.
You see it on a product page. Offer ends in nine minutes.
Your heart speeds up, and you click buy before you think.
Researchers from Princeton and the University of Chicago checked this.
They crawled about eleven thousand shopping websites.
They found tricks like these on more than twelve hundred of them.
And some countdown timers simply started over when the page reloaded.
The deadline was never real. Only the pressure was.
Urgency works because it shuts down comparison.
No time to check other stores, read reviews or sleep on it.
Here is a simple test.
When you see a timer, open the same page in a private window.
If the clock shows the same full time again, you have your answer.
Or just wait it out, and come back tomorrow.
Real sales happen again. Fake timers never really end.
Any offer that cannot survive one night of thinking was built to stop you thinking.
Close the tab and see what happens.
Follow and stop shopping on someone else's clock.

caption: Fake countdown timers on shopping sites: what a study of eleven thousand online stores found, and a simple test to spot a fake deadline.

lines.text: The smallest number on your card bill is a trap.
Every statement shows a minimum payment, often just a few percent of what you owe.
It looks like helpful advice. It works like an anchor.
A psychologist in England tested this with fake credit card bills.
Half the people saw a minimum payment on the bill. Half did not.
Among those who did not clear the whole bill, the group that saw the minimum paid back much less.
One small number pulled their payments down toward it.
Less paid means more balance left, and more interest every month.
In the United States, card statements must now show how long paying only the minimum would take.
For a big balance, it can be many years.
That box exists because the trap is real.
Here is how to cut the anchor.
Decide your payment before you open the bill.
Set an automatic payment for a fixed amount you choose, well above the minimum.
And when you can, pay the full statement balance.
The minimum keeps your account in good standing. It does not keep your money.
Follow to spot the numbers built to cost you.

caption: The minimum payment trap: why the smallest number on your credit card bill makes people pay back less, and how to cut the anchor.

lines.text: Fancy menus drop the dollar sign for a reason.
Next time, look at the prices. Just a plain eighteen, no symbol.
Researchers at Cornell tested this in a real restaurant.
Diners got one of three menus with the exact same food and prices.
One showed dollar signs. One wrote prices out in words. One showed plain numbers.
The plain number menu won.
Those diners spent significantly more than the guests whose menus had dollar signs.
The researchers suggested a simple reason.
The dollar sign reminds you that you are spending money.
A plain number feels like a score, not a cost.
Many also skip the cents, and avoid lining prices up in a column.
A column makes it easy to compare, and they would rather you read the food.
Here is the counter move.
Before you order, add the dollars back in your head.
Say the price as money. Eighteen dollars. Then decide.
And pick your budget for the meal before you open the menu.
A missing symbol cannot spend your money. Only you can.
Follow for more tricks hiding on the menu.

caption: Why fancy restaurant menus leave out the dollar sign: what a Cornell study of diners found, and the simple counter move before you order.

lines.text: Free trials are built for the day you forget.
The trial costs nothing, but they still ask for your card.
Why would a free thing need your card number?
Because the real product is the renewal.
Signing up takes one tap. Remembering to cancel takes effort, weeks later.
And doing nothing means paying.
Psychologists call it the default effect. We stick with whatever happens if we do nothing.
A research firm asked a thousand Americans to guess their monthly subscription spending.
The average guess was eighty six dollars.
When they listed every charge, the real average was two hundred nineteen dollars.
Three in four said those charges are easy to forget.
That gap is the business model.
Every forgotten month is pure profit for them.
So beat it on day one.
The moment you start a trial, set a reminder two days before it ends.
Even better, cancel right away. Many services let you keep the trial until the end.
If you forget to miss it, you never needed it.
Follow so the next free trial stays free.

caption: How free trials turn into paid subscriptions: why they ask for your card, how much people underestimate subscriptions, and how to keep a trial free.

lines.text: Many outlet products were made only for the outlet.
Outlets started as a place to sell last season's leftovers.
Then outlet malls got so big there were not enough leftovers to fill them.
So many brands started making separate lines just for outlets.
A consumer group called Consumers' Checkbook looked into it.
About half the brands they studied stocked their outlets only or mostly with different, cheaper made goods.
Cheaper fabrics, fewer details, lower prices.
In twenty fourteen, members of Congress asked the Federal Trade Commission to look into outlet price tags.
Their worry was a compare at price for items never sold in a regular store.
The deal you feel is real. The item is just a different item.
Not every outlet works this way. Some luxury brands still send real past season stock.
So how do you tell?
Check the label. Some brands add a special mark or the word factory.
Search the item number online. If it only exists at outlets, now you know.
Compare the fabric with the same piece at the regular store.
A real bargain is the same thing for less, not a lesser thing for less.
Follow to see what the price tag is not telling you.

caption: Many outlet stores sell cheaper lines made only for outlets, not leftovers, so here is how to tell a real bargain from a made for outlet item.

lines.text: One sheet of paper makes car buyers lose track.
It is called the four square, and some dealerships still use it.
A page split into four boxes.
The car's price. Your trade in. Your down payment. Your monthly payment.
You came to talk about one number. Now there are four.
Ask for a lower monthly payment, and the loan quietly gets longer.
Ask for more for your trade in, and the car's price creeps up.
Every win in one box is paid for in another.
Your monthly payment can stay where you wanted, while the total cost climbs.
It works because a brain can only juggle so much at once.
Beat it one box at a time.
Get a loan offer from your bank or credit union before you visit.
Agree on the car's total price first, including every fee.
Only then talk about your trade in, as a separate deal.
And if they push the paper back toward you, you can say no to the format.
The price you pay is one number, not four.
Follow before you sign anything with four boxes on it.

caption: The four square worksheet at car dealerships: how four boxes hide the real price of a car, and how to beat it before you sign.

lines.text: Shoppers once refused to use shopping carts.
In nineteen thirty seven, an Oklahoma grocer named Sylvan Goldman had a problem.
Customers stopped buying when their baskets got too heavy.
His idea was to let the basket carry itself.
So he put two baskets on a folding chair, and added wheels.
The first shopping cart was born. And nobody wanted it.
Women said they had pushed enough baby strollers.
Men thought it made them look less manly.
So Goldman did something clever.
He hired models to push carts around his store, pretending to shop.
Real shoppers saw others doing it, and joined in.
Within a few years, carts were everywhere.
And here is the part stores love.
A cart holds far more than you can carry, so people buy more.
Carts have kept getting bigger ever since.
Fake shoppers sold the idea. Real ones still follow the crowd.
Big stores are built around full carts, not quick trips.
If you only need a few things, skip the cart and stick to your list.
Follow for more stories about how stores shaped your habits.

caption: The surprising history of the shopping cart: in nineteen thirty seven nobody wanted it, until its inventor hired models to push carts around his store.

lines.text: Some of what you buy is just air.
There is a name for the empty space in a package. Slack fill.
Some of it has a real job.
The air in a chip bag cushions the chips so they arrive in one piece.
But some of it is there only to make the box look bigger.
In the United States, food rules call that nonfunctional slack fill.
And it counts as misleading.
Lawyers noticed. One firm counted about twenty slack fill lawsuits in two thousand eight.
By two thousand fifteen, there were more than one hundred ten.
Several targeted movie theater candy boxes.
Courts did not always agree, and plenty of cases were thrown out.
So the box is not a promise. The weight is.
Here is how to shop past the air.
Ignore the box size, and read the net weight on the label.
Compare the price per ounce on the shelf tag.
Then shake it. If it sounds empty, it probably is.
You pay for what is inside, so look inside first.
Follow for more ways packages play with your eyes.

caption: Slack fill explained: why some packages are part air, when that empty space is legal, and how to shop for what is actually inside.

lines.text: Stop reading prices in dollars. Read them in hours.
This idea comes from a classic money book called Your Money or Your Life.
It was written by Vicki Robin and Joe Dominguez, back in nineteen ninety two.
Their question is simple. What does this cost in your life?
First, find your real hourly wage.
Take what you earn, and subtract what working costs you, like commuting and work clothes.
Then divide by every hour work really takes, including the drive there and back.
For many people, the real wage is far lower than the one on paper.
Now look at that jacket.
Say it costs one hundred twenty dollars, and you really keep fifteen an hour.
That jacket is eight hours of your life.
A full working day, for one jacket.
Some things are still worth it. Many suddenly are not.
Dollars feel abstract. Hours feel like your life.
Do the math once, write your number on your phone, and check it before every big buy.
Your time is the one thing you cannot earn back.
Follow for money tricks that work for you, not against you.

caption: Price it in hours of work: the classic money trick from Your Money or Your Life that turns every price tag into hours of your life.

lines.text: Some cheap store brands are made by famous brands.
Look at certain bags of Costco's Kirkland coffee.
Right on the label, it says roasted by Starbucks.
Same roaster. Different bag. A much lower price per ounce.
Coffee is just one example of a common deal.
Why would a big brand make a cheaper copy of itself?
Because factories are expensive, and idle machines make nothing.
Selling extra to a store brand keeps production running.
And if they do not make it, a competitor will.
Usually you will not see the maker's name, though.
But you have clues.
Check the ingredients list. Same order, same ingredients is a good sign.
For medicine, compare the active ingredient and the dose.
In the United States, a generic medicine must have the same active ingredient as the brand.
Then let your own taste test decide.
Try the store brand once. If you cannot tell, you just found a raise.
Paying extra for a logo is a choice. Make it on purpose.
Follow to find out what you are really paying for.

caption: Store brands made by big brands: why some cheap labels come from famous makers, like coffee roasted by Starbucks, and the clues that give it away.

lines.text: Your brain reads prices left to right, and stops early.
Three ninety nine feels much closer to three than to four.
Even though it is one cent away from four.
Researchers call this the left digit effect.
Your brain grabs the first number and anchors on it.
It is not just in stores. Economists found it in used cars.
They studied more than twenty two million car sales at auctions.
Prices dropped sharply every time the odometer crossed a new ten thousand mile mark.
A car with forty nine thousand nine hundred miles sold for noticeably more than one with fifty thousand.
Same car. Same wear. One digit changed.
There is also an old story about cashiers.
Odd prices supposedly forced them to open the register and give change, so they could not pocket the cash.
Nobody has proved that one. The left digit effect is well documented.
So here is the habit.
When you see ninety nine, round up out loud.
Nineteen ninety nine is twenty. Four ninety nine is five.
The store is counting on your eyes. Use your math.
Follow for more tricks hiding inside a price tag.

caption: Why prices end in ninety nine: the left digit effect, the used car study that proves it, and the old cashier theory nobody has proven.

lines.text: The second cheapest wine is not the rip off.
You have probably heard this one.
Diners are too embarrassed to order the cheapest bottle.
So they order the second cheapest, and restaurants supposedly mark that one up the most.
Two economists finally tested it.
They collected wine lists from about two hundred fifty London restaurants.
Then they compared each bottle's price with what it costs in shops.
The second cheapest bottle was not the worst deal.
The myth was simply wrong.
Its markup was clearly lower than the bottles just above it.
The biggest markups sat in the middle of the list.
Exactly where people feel safe ordering.
The study only covered London, so your city may differ.
But the lesson travels well.
The real profit hides where you stop paying attention.
Next time, ask the server which bottle they would drink.
Or compare the price with what one bottle costs in a store, using your phone.
A great wine at a fair price beats a famous label every single time.
Follow for more myths about prices, tested.

caption: Is the second cheapest wine a rip off? Economists checked wine lists from about two hundred fifty London restaurants and found the myth was wrong.

lines.text: People rate the same cookie higher when there are fewer.
In nineteen seventy five, psychologists ran a simple test with cookie jars.
Some people got a jar with ten cookies. Others got a jar with two.
Same cookies. Same jar.
The cookies from the nearly empty jar were rated as more desirable.
Scarcity made the cookie better, without changing a single crumb.
Online stores know this feeling very well.
Only two left. Low stock. Selling fast.
Researchers who scanned thousands of shopping sites found some of these messages were not true.
On some sites, the low stock warning showed up no matter what.
The message was there to make you hurry, not to inform you.
So, slow down on purpose.
Ask yourself if you would still want it with a hundred left.
If the answer is no, the scarcity was doing the selling.
And if it truly sells out, there is almost always something just as good.
Wanting something because it is rare is how stores sell ordinary things.
Follow so fake scarcity stops working on you.

caption: Why only two left in stock makes you buy: the famous cookie jar experiment on scarcity, and what researchers found on real shopping sites.

lines.text: A free head start makes you spend more.
Researchers handed out loyalty cards at a car wash.
One card needed eight stamps for a free wash.
The other needed ten stamps, but came with two already stamped.
Both cards needed exactly eight more washes.
Yet the head start card was finished almost twice as often.
Feeling partly done pulls you to the finish.
It is called the endowed progress effect.
And there is a second trick inside every punch card.
Another study found that coffee buyers came back faster as they got closer to their free drink.
The closer the goal, the faster we run.
That free coffee is not really free.
It is paid for by the extra visits you would not have made.
Loyalty cards are fine if you were coming anyway.
Just notice when a card starts choosing your coffee shop for you.
Or when you buy one more, only to fill the card.
A stamp is a reward. It should never become a reason.
Follow for more loyalty tricks hiding in your wallet.

caption: Why coffee punch cards work so well: the car wash experiment behind the endowed progress effect, and when a loyalty card starts spending for you.

lines.text: Building something yourself makes you overvalue it.
Researchers gave people a plain storage box from IKEA, flat packed.
Some built it themselves. Others got the exact same box, already built.
Then everyone said what they would pay for it.
The builders were willing to pay about sixty three percent more.
Same box. Same screws. More love.
The researchers called it the IKEA effect.
Your effort becomes part of the price you feel.
But only if you finish.
People who did not complete their build did not get the boost.
Meal kits, build your own toys and custom designs all ask for a little of your effort.
And a little effort makes the result feel worth more.
It is also why your homemade things feel priceless, and nobody else agrees.
So when you build, customize or assemble, add one question.
Would I pay this price for it if someone else had made it?
If not, that extra value lives only in your head.
Love what you build. Just do not overpay for the feeling.
Follow for more tricks your own brain plays on you.

caption: The IKEA effect: why people who built their own furniture were willing to pay about sixty three percent more for it, and how to avoid overpaying.

lines.text: Splitting a price into four makes it feel smaller.
A two hundred dollar jacket becomes four payments of fifty.
Fifty feels easy. Two hundred did not.
Same jacket. Same total. A much smaller pain at checkout.
That is the whole idea of buy now, pay later.
And it is working.
America's consumer finance watchdog warned that many users may spend more than they otherwise would.
It also found that most borrowers had several loans open at once at some point in a year.
Four payments here, four payments there.
Each one looks small. Together they can quietly eat your paycheck.
And a Federal Reserve survey found about one in four users paid late in twenty twenty four.
Late fees turn the free loan into an expensive one.
Here is a simple rule.
Only split a purchase you could pay in full today.
If you could not afford it once, you cannot afford it four times.
And keep one list of every plan you have open.
Later always comes. Make sure it finds you ready.
Follow to see the real price behind the easy payments.

caption: Buy now pay later explained: why four small payments feel cheaper, what regulators found about stacking loans and late payments, and one simple rule.

lines.text: Almost winning makes you want to play again.
Two cherries line up, and the third stops just past the line.
So close. You can almost taste the jackpot.
But a near miss is just a miss.
Scientists at the University of Cambridge scanned people's brains while they played a simple slot game.
Near misses felt worse than clear losses.
Yet they made people want to keep playing.
And they lit up the same reward areas as real wins.
Your brain treats almost as a step toward winning.
When players felt in control, like stopping the reel themselves, the effect got stronger.
Here is the cold truth.
Each spin is decided by a random number generator.
The last spin does not make the next one closer.
Close does not exist inside a machine. Only win or lose.
So treat every near miss as a full loss, because that is what it was.
And set your stop limit before you sit down, not after a so close moment.
The machine wants you chasing almost. Walk away from it.
Follow to see the next trick before it plays you.

caption: Why near misses on slot machines keep you playing: what a Cambridge brain scan study found about almost winning, and the cold truth about every spin.

lines.text: A famous slogan sold the diamond engagement ring.
In nineteen thirty eight, the diamond giant De Beers hired an American ad agency.
Its own surveys found many young men saw engagement rings as an unnecessary luxury.
So the agency set out to change the story.
In nineteen forty seven, a copywriter named Frances Gerety wrote four words.
A diamond is forever.
The line tied diamonds to lasting love, and quietly discouraged anyone from reselling them.
Advertising Age later named it the slogan of the century.
Later ads even suggested how much to spend, using months of salary.
That rule never came from tradition. It came from marketing.
And resale is the painful part.
Try selling a diamond, and you will often be offered a small fraction of what you paid.
Today, lab grown diamonds are the same material, for much less money.
None of this means rings are bad.
It means the price of love was set by an ad agency, and you are allowed to rewrite it.
Spend what fits your life, not a number from an old campaign.
Follow for more stories behind the things we buy.

caption: How a diamond is forever sold the engagement ring: the nineteen forty seven slogan, the salary rule that came from ads, and the truth about resale.

lines.text: A student sent Pepsi a check for a fighter jet.
In the mid nineteen nineties, Pepsi ran a points promotion.
Drink Pepsi, collect points, trade them for a shirt or sunglasses.
Then the commercial ended with a military Harrier jet, for seven million points.
It was meant as a joke. One student did the math.
The rules let you buy extra points for ten cents each.
Seven million points came to about seven hundred thousand dollars.
A real Harrier was worth tens of millions.
So John Leonard found investors and mailed Pepsi a check for about seven hundred thousand dollars.
Pepsi said no, and the case went to court.
In nineteen ninety nine, a federal judge ruled for Pepsi.
No reasonable person, she said, could think the ad was a real offer.
Pepsi changed the ad to seven hundred million points, just in case.
The lesson is not about jets.
Promotions are written by lawyers, and the fine print usually wins.
So before you chase a prize, read the rules like he did.
Just expect the company to read them better.
Follow for more wild stories from the history of money.

caption: The Pepsi points jet: how a student sent Pepsi a check for about seven hundred thousand dollars to claim a Harrier fighter jet, and what the court said.

lines.text: Bulb makers once fined companies whose bulbs lasted too long.
In nineteen twenty four, the biggest light bulb companies met in Geneva.
They formed a cartel called Phoebus.
And they agreed on a target life for ordinary bulbs. One thousand hours.
Bulbs were sent to a lab in Switzerland for testing.
Makers whose bulbs lasted longer than allowed paid fines.
Within a decade, the average bulb life had dropped by about a third.
Shorter life meant more bulbs sold.
This is the most famous case of planned obsolescence.
Products designed, or managed, to wear out sooner than they could.
It is not just history.
In twenty seventeen, Apple admitted slowing some older iPhones with aging batteries.
Apple said it was to prevent sudden shutdowns.
It later agreed to pay up to five hundred million dollars to settle a lawsuit in America.
So how do you push back?
Before buying, check if the battery can be replaced, and how long updates are promised.
Look up repair scores and spare part prices, not just the sticker price.
The cheapest product is the one you do not have to buy twice.
Follow for more tricks built into the things you own.

caption: Planned obsolescence: the nineteen twenty four light bulb cartel that fined makers for long lasting bulbs, the iPhone battery case, and how to buy things that last.

lines.text: Give every want one night before you buy it.
This is the twenty four hour rule, and it is simple.
When you want something you did not plan to buy, you wait a full day.
No cart. No saved card. Just a note with the item and the price.
Tomorrow, you look at the note and decide again.
Why does it work?
Impulse buys run on a rush of excitement, and that rush fades.
Stores design the moment of purchase to happen before it does.
Countdowns, limited stock, one tap checkout. All built for right now.
Even the law admits pressure works.
In the United States, a federal rule gives you three days to cancel some sales made at your home.
Door to door sellers were so good at pressure that buyers needed time to think twice.
You can give yourself that same protection for free.
If you still want it tomorrow, buy it without guilt.
If you forgot about it, you just saved the full price.
Either way, you decided. Not the store.
Follow for more money habits that actually stick.

caption: The twenty four hour rule: why waiting one night beats impulse buying, what the law already admits about sales pressure, and how to use it.

lines.text: Your snacks are shrinking, and the price is not.
It is called shrinkflation.
Same box, same price, a little less inside.
A few chips fewer. A thinner bar. A bottle that holds a bit less.
Companies do it because people notice price changes much more than size changes.
Raise the price, and shoppers complain. Shrink the pack, and most never see it.
But some governments noticed.
In twenty twenty four, France made big stores post a warning next to products that shrank.
The sign has to say how much less you get, and how much the real price went up.
Products from some of the biggest snack brands showed up on those lists.
In the United States, official inflation numbers count a smaller pack as a price increase.
So the trick does not fool the statisticians. It only fools shoppers.
Here is how not to be one of them.
Ignore the front of the pack. Look at the net weight.
Then check the price per ounce on the shelf tag.
When a favorite suddenly feels lighter, compare it with the store brand.
The price did not change. The deal did.
Follow so the next shrink does not get past you.

caption: Shrinkflation explained: why packs get smaller while prices stay the same, how France forced stores to warn shoppers, and how to spot it yourself.

lines.text: Fees shown at the last step make you spend more.
It is called drip pricing.
You see a ticket for fifty dollars. At checkout, it is sixty eight.
Service fee. Facility fee. Processing fee.
Economists tested this on millions of shoppers at a ticket site called StubHub.
Some saw the full price from the start. Others saw fees only at checkout.
The group that met the fees late spent about twenty one percent more.
They also bought more often, and picked more expensive seats.
Once you have chosen and imagined the show, quitting feels like losing it.
After the test, the site moved its fees to the end for everyone.
Regulators noticed.
Since twenty twenty five, a federal rule makes ticket sellers and hotels show the total price up front.
But plenty of other sites still drip.
Here is your defense.
Before you fall in love with a choice, click all the way to the final checkout page.
Compare final totals, never starting prices.
A price is only real once every fee has shown up.
Follow for more tricks hiding between the first click and the last.

caption: Drip pricing explained: in a huge StubHub experiment, people spent about twenty one percent more when fees appeared only at checkout, and here is your defense.

lines.text: Tip screens now ask you everywhere, even for a muffin.
You grab a coffee, and the screen swings toward you.
Twenty percent. Twenty five. Thirty.
The cashier is watching. The people behind you are waiting.
That pressure is the design.
Pew Research surveyed almost twelve thousand Americans about tipping in twenty twenty three.
Seventy two percent said tipping is now expected in more places than five years before.
Only about a third said it was easy to know when and how much to tip.
And more people opposed suggested tip amounts on screens than supported them.
The suggested buttons are an anchor.
Studies of taxi screens found higher preset options pushed average tips up.
Here is how to tip on your terms.
Decide your tipping rules before you are at the counter.
For example, your usual tip for table service, and your own amount at the counter.
Then use the custom button without apology.
Tipping is a thank you, not a toll booth.
A screen cannot judge you. It can only suggest.
Follow for more tricks at the checkout.

caption: Tip screens everywhere: what a Pew survey of almost twelve thousand Americans found about tipping pressure, and how to tip on your own terms.

lines.text: A travel site once showed Mac users pricier hotels first.
In twenty twelve, the Wall Street Journal looked at the travel site Orbitz.
Orbitz had found that Mac users spent twenty to thirty dollars more a night on hotels.
They were also more likely to book four and five star rooms.
So the site tested putting pricier hotels higher in the results for Mac users.
The same room did not cost more. It was just shown first.
And most people book something near the top of the list.
Your computer, phone and location can all shape what a site shows you.
This is called steering.
It is usually legal, and very common.
The order of results is a sales decision, not a ranking of value.
So take the wheel back.
Sort by price yourself, from lowest to highest.
Filter for what you need, like location and rating, then compare.
And check the same hotel on a second site, or the hotel's own website.
The top result is the one they want you to pick. Not always the one you should.
Follow for more tricks hiding in what you see first.

caption: When Orbitz showed Mac users pricier hotels first: the twenty twelve steering experiment, and how to take back control of search results when you book.

lines.text: A tiny reward can make you spend a lot more.
Economists at the Chicago Fed studied a cash back card program.
The reward was just one percent back.
Yet in the first months, people spent about sixty eight dollars more a month.
And their card debt grew by about one hundred fifteen dollars a month.
To earn a few cents, they spent dollars.
Some of it was spending moved from other cards. But the debt was real.
Points are even harder to judge than cash.
Is a point worth one cent? Half a cent? Nobody knows at checkout.
And programs can change what points are worth, whenever their rules allow.
Meanwhile, the progress bar toward the next reward keeps you swiping.
Here is the rule that keeps rewards working for you.
Only use a rewards card for things you already planned to buy.
Pay the full balance every month, or the interest eats the rewards.
And never buy something because it earns double points.
Double points on something you did not need is still a loss.
Rewards are a discount, not a reason to shop.
Follow so the rewards stop rewarding them instead of you.

caption: Why credit card points make you spend more: a Chicago Fed study of a one percent cash back card, and the simple rule that keeps rewards working for you.

lines.text: Mail in rebates count on you forgetting.
The sign says fifty dollars back. The fine print says mail the form.
With the receipt. And the barcode. Within thirty days.
In the industry, unclaimed rebates have a name. Breakage.
Estimates vary, but trade reports often say forty to sixty percent are never claimed.
A United States senator once said about half of rebates go unredeemed.
And people are bad at predicting their own follow through.
Research shows buyers overestimate how likely they are to claim a rebate.
So the rebate sells the product, and the forms keep the money.
One study even found that giving people more time made them less likely to claim.
More time felt like permission to wait, until it was too late.
So here is the rebate rule.
Judge the price without the rebate. Would you still buy it?
If yes, fill in the form the same day, before you even open the box.
Take a photo of everything you send.
A rebate is only a discount once the check clears.
Follow to catch the next trick hiding in the fine print.

caption: Why mail in rebates go unclaimed: what breakage means, why more time made people less likely to claim, and the simple rebate rule to follow.

lines.text: Scientists watched brains decide whether to buy.
In a famous study, people shopped inside a brain scanner.
Twenty six volunteers made real purchase choices with money from the researchers.
They saw a product, then its price, then chose to buy or not.
Liking the product lit up a reward area.
But when the price felt too high, an area called the insula became active.
The insula is linked to anticipating loss and discomfort.
Those signals helped predict who would buy.
Researchers call this tug of war the pain of paying.
And here is why it matters.
Many modern ways to pay make that pain softer.
Cards, phone taps, saved details, subscriptions, all inclusive bundles.
When paying stops hurting, spending stops feeling like a decision.
The pain is not your enemy. It is your brakes.
So add a little friction back.
Remove saved cards from shopping apps.
For big buys, look at the full price out loud, or in cash terms, before paying.
A little pain now can save a lot of regret later.
Follow for more ways your brain and your wallet fight.

caption: The pain of paying: what a famous brain scan study found when people decided whether to buy, and why a little payment pain is good for you.

lines.text: No interest is not the same as zero interest.
You see it at furniture stores and electronics shops.
No interest if paid in full in twelve months.
It sounds like a free loan. Read it again.
This is called deferred interest.
The interest is not gone. It is quietly counted from day one.
Pay off every cent in time, and you owe nothing extra.
Miss by one dollar, or one day, and all that interest can land at once.
Often at store card rates of twenty five percent or more.
Most people do pay in time, according to the consumer finance watchdog.
But a sizable share do not, especially people with lower credit scores.
The watchdog even urged stores to switch to true zero percent offers instead.
With those, interest only starts on what is left after the promo.
So here is the move.
Divide the price by the promo months, minus one, and pay that every month.
Set it as an automatic payment, so the deadline never surprises you.
And if you cannot clear it in time, do not use the offer.
A free loan with a deadline is only free if you beat it.
Follow so the fine print stops winning.

caption: Deferred interest explained: why no interest if paid in full is not zero interest, what happens if you miss by one dollar, and how to beat the deadline.

lines.text: Your phone does not need to listen to you.
You talk about hiking boots, and an hour later, there is an ad for boots.
It feels like proof. So researchers checked.
A team at Northeastern University tested more than seventeen thousand popular apps.
They found no evidence of apps secretly turning on the microphone for ads.
In twenty twenty six, American regulators made a media company pay for falsely claiming its ad service could hear conversations.
But some apps were sending screenshots and recordings of the screen to other companies.
So the real tracking is quieter than a microphone.
Your location, your searches, your friends' searches, the stores you walk past.
That is usually enough to guess what you were talking about.
And then there is a trick your brain plays.
Once something is on your mind, you notice it everywhere.
It is called the frequency illusion.
Here is how to make the guessing harder.
Turn off ad personalization in your phone and account settings.
Limit location access to while using the app.
And take a minute to check which apps can see your screen and microphone.
Follow so the next creepy ad has fewer clues.

caption: Is your phone listening to you? What a study of seventeen thousand apps found, what regulators said in twenty twenty six, and how ads really guess your conversations.

lines.text: That cheap Thanksgiving turkey is bait.
Every November, stores slash turkey prices, sometimes below what they paid.
Some even give one away when you spend enough.
It is called a loss leader.
The store loses on the bird, and wins on everything around it.
Stuffing. Cranberries. Pie. Wine. Candles. A new roasting pan.
The turkey gets you in the door. The cart pays for it.
In twenty twenty five, the American Farm Bureau priced a classic dinner for ten at about fifty five dollars.
The turkey alone averaged about twenty one dollars, its smallest share of the bill since two thousand.
So the bird is rarely what blows the budget.
It is the extras that ride along in the cart.
Here is the plan.
Write the full menu first, and buy only what is on it.
Grab the turkey deal, then walk past the holiday displays.
Check what is already in your pantry before you shop.
Let the store lose money on the turkey. Do not make it up for them.
Follow for more holiday tricks before they reach your cart.

caption: Why stores sell Thanksgiving turkeys so cheap: the loss leader trick, what the Farm Bureau found about dinner costs, and how to keep the extras out of your cart.

lines.text: Casino chips are not quite the trick you think.
The popular story says chips feel like toy money, so you bet more.
It sounds right. The truth is more interesting.
Casinos love chips for practical reasons first.
They are faster to stack and count than bills.
They are harder to steal, and easier to spot when fake.
Since two thousand five, some casinos even put tracking chips inside them.
Now the money question.
When researchers tested gamblers on real slot machines, paying with cash or casino vouchers did not change bet sizes.
So at least on slots, the toy money effect looked weaker than the legend.
But payment format still matters elsewhere.
Studies with credit cards show people often spend more when money feels less real.
And chips hide one thing very well. Your running total.
A stack of colorful discs is hard to translate into rent and groceries.
So do the translation yourself.
Decide your limit in dollars before you buy any chips.
And count what is left in dollars, not in stacks.
Follow for more myths and truths about how casinos work.

caption: Do casino chips make you bet more? Why casinos really use chips, what a slot machine experiment found, and the one thing chips hide very well.

lines.text: Black Friday deals are often not the best price.
A British consumer group called Which tracked Black Friday prices.
They followed the same products for six months before and after.
In one year, ninety eight percent of the deals were the same price or cheaper at other times.
The next year, it was still about nine in ten.
So what is Black Friday really selling?
Urgency. Crowds. Countdown clocks. The feeling that you must buy today.
Doorbusters are often limited to a handful of units per store.
They pull you in, and the rest of the store does the selling.
And some was prices are not the price anyone actually paid.
Here is how to shop it like a pro.
Make your list before the ads start.
Check each item's price history with a price tracker.
If the deal is only good compared with a fake was price, skip it.
And if you did not need it in October, you probably do not need it now.
The best Black Friday deal is the thing you did not buy.
Follow for more tricks before the holiday sales hit.

caption: Black Friday deals exposed: a consumer group found nine in ten were the same price or cheaper at other times, and here is how to shop smart.

lines.text: Say the word wedding, and some prices go up.
Couples call it the wedding tax.
Consumer Reports decided to test it with secret shoppers.
They asked vendors for quotes on two events that were exactly the same.
Same size, same services, same everything.
One was called a wedding. The other, an anniversary party.
In more than a quarter of cases, the wedding got the higher price.
The biggest gaps came from limousine companies and photographers.
Some vendors say weddings truly need more work and more pressure.
Sometimes that is fair. But the same car for the same hours is still the same car.
And few couples want to haggle over their big day.
That is exactly why the markup works.
So here is the smart move.
Ask for itemized quotes, and compare them with prices for other events.
Get three quotes for every service, in writing.
Look at off season dates and weekday events, which are often cheaper.
Your love story is priceless. The limo is not.
Follow for more prices that change with one word.

caption: The wedding tax is real for some vendors: Consumer Reports secret shoppers found wedding quotes were higher in more than a quarter of cases, and how to avoid it.

lines.text: Black Friday was never named for profits.
You have probably heard the story.
Stores finally go into the black, meaning profit, the day after Thanksgiving.
It is a nice story. It came decades too late.
The name started with police officers in Philadelphia, in the nineteen fifties and sixties.
The day after Thanksgiving brought huge crowds of shoppers downtown.
And the famous Army Navy football game was played that Saturday.
Traffic jams, packed sidewalks, shoplifters, chaos.
Officers had to work long shifts, and they gave the day a dark name.
Some had their days off canceled.
Black Friday.
Merchants hated it. They even tried to rename it Big Friday.
It did not stick.
The happier profit story only shows up in print around nineteen eighty one.
Retailers took a name about chaos and sold it back to us as a party.
Today it is one of the biggest shopping days of the year in America.
So when the crowds and countdowns start, remember the original meaning.
It was a warning, not a celebration.
Follow for more surprising stories behind how we shop.

caption: Where Black Friday got its name: not from profits, but from Philadelphia police who dreaded the crowds and traffic the day after Thanksgiving.

lines.text: The cheaper item is often the more expensive one.
Meet cost per use. Price divided by how many times you use it.
Take two pairs of boots.
One costs forty dollars and falls apart after one winter.
Say you wear it forty times. That is one dollar per wear.
The other costs one hundred sixty dollars and lasts five winters.
Two hundred wears. Eighty cents per wear.
The expensive pair was the cheaper one.
It works the other way too.
A gym membership at fifty dollars a month, used twice, is twenty five dollars a visit.
That dress for an event you attend once? One wear, full price.
Stores sell you the sticker price. You live with the cost per use.
Here is how to use it.
Before buying, guess honestly how many times you will use it.
Divide the price by that number.
If the number looks bad, wait, borrow or rent instead.
Spend more on what you use daily, and less on what you use once.
Follow for more money math that stores hope you skip.

caption: Cost per use explained: why a one hundred sixty dollar pair of boots can be cheaper than a forty dollar pair, and how to do the math before you buy.

lines.text: A vacuum company gave away flights and lost millions.
In nineteen ninety two, Hoover's British branch had a brilliant idea.
Spend at least one hundred pounds on Hoover products, and get two free return flights.
First to Europe, then even to America.
The flights were worth far more than the vacuum cleaners.
So people bought vacuums they did not need, just for the tickets.
Factories ran extra shifts to keep up.
Then came the problem. Hundreds of thousands wanted to fly.
Hoover made redemption harder, and customers got angry.
Court cases dragged on until nineteen ninety eight.
The top managers of the British arm were fired.
In the end, the promotion cost tens of millions of pounds.
And the brand's reputation took the bigger hit.
The lesson for shoppers is the flip side.
When a free gift is worth more than the product, read the conditions twice.
Either the company made a huge mistake, or the gift is very hard to claim.
Usually, it is the second one.
Follow for more promotions that went spectacularly wrong.

caption: The Hoover free flights fiasco: how a nineteen ninety two vacuum promotion offering free flights to Europe and America cost tens of millions of pounds.

lines.text: The best shelf spot is often paid for.
Walk down any aisle and look straight ahead.
The products at eye level are rarely there by accident.
Brands often pay stores for good placement. These payments are called slotting fees.
Why pay? Because where you look decides what you buy.
Researchers tracked shoppers' eyes in front of real shelves.
Brands placed near the center of the shelf got more attention, and were rated better.
And having more rows of the same product on the shelf mattered even more.
Older studies found that doubling shelf space could lift a product's sales by about a third.
So the shelf is a battle, and you are the prize.
Here is how to shop the whole shelf.
Look up, and look down.
Store brands and cheaper sizes often sit on the bottom shelf.
Compare the unit price across every row, not just the one in front of you.
The easiest product to see is rarely the best deal to buy.
Bend your knees. Save your money.
Follow for more ways stores guide your eyes.

caption: Why the products at eye level are there: slotting fees, an eye tracking study of real shelves, and why the best deal is often on the bottom shelf.

lines.text: Cyber Monday was invented in a press release.
In two thousand five, an online retail group coined the name in a press release.
The idea was that people shopped online from work the Monday after Thanksgiving.
Today it is the biggest online shopping day in America.
In twenty twenty five, Americans spent about fourteen billion dollars online in one day.
At the peak, that was about sixteen million dollars a minute.
And over a billion of it was paid with buy now, pay later.
That last number tells you how the day works.
Cyber Monday is built for speed.
Saved cards. One click. Flash deals that last an hour.
Every step that used to make you pause has been removed.
And many deals simply continue from Black Friday, with a new name.
Here is how to keep your head.
Shop from a list you made before the weekend.
Leave items in your cart overnight, and see if you still want them.
Check the price history, and skip any deal that needs paying later.
The day was named to sell. You do not have to buy.
Follow so the next big sale day does not spend for you.

caption: Cyber Monday tricks: how a retail group named the day in two thousand five, the record spending in twenty twenty five, and how to keep your head.

lines.text: The same wine tastes better with a higher price.
Scientists at Caltech and Stanford ran a sneaky wine tasting.
People sipped wines inside a brain scanner, each with a price.
But one wine was served twice. Once at ninety dollars. Once at ten.
Same liquid. Only the price changed.
People said the ninety dollar version tasted better.
And it was not just politeness.
A brain area linked to pleasure was more active for the expensive one.
The price did not just change their opinion. It changed the experience.
Now flip it.
In a large series of blind tastings, regular drinkers slightly preferred the cheaper wines.
Without a price tag, expensive did not win.
So the expensive taste was partly in the head, not the glass.
This works far beyond wine.
The same may happen with other treats sold on prestige.
Want to test yourself?
Have a friend pour a cheap and an expensive bottle without telling you which is which.
If you cannot tell, you just found a cheaper favorite.
Follow for more ways a price tag changes what you feel.

caption: Why expensive wine tastes better: the brain scan study where the same wine tasted better at ninety dollars, and what blind tastings found.

lines.text: Louder bar music made people drink faster.
French researchers ran a simple test in two bars.
On some evenings the music was at a normal level.
On others, it was turned up loud.
They quietly watched young men drinking beer.
With loud music, the average went from about two and a half drinks to almost three and a half.
And each glass was finished about three minutes faster.
Same bar. Same beer. Only the volume changed.
The researchers suggested two reasons.
Loud music can raise excitement, and excited people drink faster.
And when you cannot hear each other, you talk less and sip more.
It was a small study, so it is a clue, not a law.
But many venues control music on purpose, from tempo to volume.
So set your own pace.
Decide how many drinks you will have before you walk in.
Order water between rounds, and put your glass down between sips.
Step outside to talk, where you can actually hear each other.
The playlist is not just for fun. It is part of the bill.
Follow for more tricks you can hear but never notice.

caption: Why bars play loud music: a French study found louder music made young men drink more and faster, and how to set your own pace on a night out.

lines.text: Some websites are designed to trick your clicks.
A designer named Harry Brignull gave these tricks a name in twenty ten.
Dark patterns.
A gray button to say no, and a big bright one to say yes.
No thanks, I prefer paying full price. That one is called confirmshaming.
Extra items that sneak into your cart. Boxes already ticked for you.
Easy to sign up. A maze to cancel.
In twenty twenty two, the Federal Trade Commission published a whole report on these tricks.
The same year, Epic Games agreed to pay two hundred forty five million dollars in refunds to players.
Regulators said Fortnite's design pushed people into unwanted purchases.
And in Europe, a law in force since twenty twenty four bans dark patterns on online platforms.
But they have not disappeared. They have just become quieter.
Here is how to spot them.
Read the small gray link before the big bright button.
Check every box before you pay, and your cart before you confirm.
If leaving feels harder than joining, that is the design talking.
Slow down. Their whole trick is your speed.
Follow so the next button cannot fool you.

caption: Dark patterns explained: the design tricks that push your clicks, what the FTC and the Fortnite case revealed, and how to spot them before you pay.

lines.text: Some car makers tried to rent you your own car.
The hardware is already in the car. You just pay to switch it on.
In twenty twenty two, BMW offered heated seats as a monthly subscription in some countries.
The heaters were already built into the seats.
Drivers hated it. Few people signed up.
In twenty twenty three, BMW dropped the idea for one time payments.
Mercedes tried something bolder with some of its electric cars in America.
Pay twelve hundred dollars a year, and the car accelerates faster.
The motor could always do it. The software held it back.
Why do companies love this?
One payment ends. A subscription keeps paying, year after year.
And it can turn features you already paid to build into new monthly bills.
Before you buy any car, ask one question.
Which features need a subscription, now or after a free trial?
Read the connected services terms, and how much each one costs per year.
Then add five years of those fees to the price.
If you own the car, you should own what is inside it.
Follow for more tricks hiding in the things you pay for monthly.

caption: Car features by subscription: BMW heated seats, the Mercedes acceleration upgrade for twelve hundred dollars a year, and the question to ask before you buy a car.

lines.text: A store dropped its endless sales and customers left.
This is a true story about a famous American store.
In twenty twelve, JCPenney hired Ron Johnson, the man behind the Apple Stores.
He saw prices set high only to be marked down with coupons.
So he replaced them with honest everyday prices.
Same products, often for the same final price. Just no sale signs.
Customers hated it.
Revenue fell about twenty five percent in one year.
The company lost nearly a billion dollars.
Johnson was pushed out after about sixteen months.
And the coupons came back.
Why would people prefer a sale price to the same low price?
Because a sale is not just a price. It is a win.
Seeing forty percent off feels like you beat the store.
A plain low price feels like nothing happened.
Stores know you will pay extra for that feeling of winning.
So ignore the percent off, and look only at the final price.
Would you pay that without the red sign? Then it is a good deal.
Follow for more stories of when shoppers' feelings beat logic.

caption: When JCPenney dropped its sales in twenty twelve, revenue fell about twenty five percent, and here is why a sale feels better than the same low price.

lines.text: One new robe started a famous philosopher's spending spree.
Denis Diderot was a French philosopher in the seventeen hundreds.
One day, he received a beautiful scarlet dressing gown.
Suddenly, everything around him looked shabby next to it.
His old chair. His rug. His desk.
So he replaced them, one by one, to match the robe.
He wrote that he had mastered his old robe, but became a slave to the new one.
In nineteen eighty eight, an anthropologist named this the Diderot effect.
One new thing makes the rest feel wrong, and buying spirals.
You know this one.
A new sofa needs new cushions. Then a new rug. Then a lamp.
A new phone needs a new case, new earbuds, a new charger.
Stores love it. That is why the matching items sit right next to each other.
Here is how to stop the spiral.
Before a big buy, list what else you will feel pushed to replace.
Add those prices to the first one. That is the real cost.
And give yourself one week before buying any matching extra.
Follow for more money traps with famous names.

caption: The Diderot effect: how one new robe made a French philosopher replace everything he owned, and how to stop the buying spiral after a big purchase.

lines.text: Abroad, the card machine asks a costly question.
Pay in euros, or in dollars?
Dollars sounds safer. You know exactly what you are paying.
It feels like the honest option.
That choice has a name. Dynamic currency conversion.
When you pick your home currency, the exchange rate is set by the shop's payment provider.
Not by your bank. And it is usually worse.
Consumer groups have found extra costs of a few percent.
One investigation found markups as high as twelve percent.
On a two thousand dollar trip, that can be a nice dinner, gone.
The same trick waits at airport cash machines and some hotels.
Some machines even show the home currency first, to nudge you.
The rule is simple.
Always pay in the local currency.
Let your own card network convert it. It is usually the better rate.
If a cashier chooses for you, ask them to run it again in local money.
And bring a card with no foreign transaction fees if you can.
Feeling familiar should never cost you extra.
Follow for more travel money tricks.

caption: Pay in your own currency abroad? Why dynamic currency conversion at the card machine usually costs more, and the simple rule to always pay in local currency.

lines.text: Malls are designed to make you forget why you came.
There is a name for the moment it happens. The Gruen transfer.
It is named after Victor Gruen, the architect of America's first enclosed mall.
Southdale Center opened in Minnesota in nineteen fifty six.
Gruen dreamed of a town center, with gardens, a post office and a library.
Developers kept the shops and dropped most of the rest.
The Gruen transfer is the moment you lose track of your plan.
No windows. No clocks you notice. Paths that curve past more stores.
You walk in for one thing, and slowly start browsing for everything.
The irony? Gruen hated what malls became.
In nineteen seventy eight, he publicly disowned the mall developments that followed him.
But the name stuck, and so did the design.
Here is how to stay on track.
Know the one store you need, and check the map before you walk.
Go straight there, and set a time to leave.
If you want to browse, browse on purpose, with a budget.
A mall is a maze with free entry and expensive exits.
Follow for more tricks hidden in the buildings around you.

caption: The Gruen transfer: the moment a mall makes you forget why you came, named after the architect of the first enclosed mall, who later disowned malls.

lines.text: One country ruled some video game loot boxes were gambling.
A loot box is a mystery prize you pay for inside a game.
You do not know what is inside until you open it.
Maybe a rare skin. Probably something you already have.
In twenty eighteen, Belgium's gaming authority looked at popular games.
It found that paid loot boxes in some of them broke the country's gambling laws.
The Netherlands also ruled that some loot boxes were a form of gambling.
Researchers in Britain surveyed more than seven thousand gamers.
The more people spent on loot boxes, the more serious their gambling problems tended to be.
That does not prove one causes the other. But the link was clear.
The design borrows from slot machines.
Spinning reveals, flashing colors, and rare prizes that almost land.
And games often hide the real price behind gems or coins.
Here is how to protect your wallet, or your kid's.
Turn off in game purchases in the console or phone settings.
Convert every pack of gems back into real money before you buy.
And if a prize needs luck, decide your limit before you start.
A surprise you pay for is still a bet.
Follow for more tricks inside the games you love.

caption: Are loot boxes gambling? Belgium said some were, a study of seven thousand gamers found a link to problem gambling, and here is how to protect your wallet.

lines.text: The free vacation comes with a sales pitch.
Free hotel nights, show tickets or a dinner, if you attend a short presentation.
Short can turn into hours.
It is a timeshare sale.
You buy a slice of a vacation property, usually one week a year.
The pitch is built on emotion. Sunsets, family photos, a happy room.
Then comes the pressure. This price is only for today.
And the costs do not stop at the price.
Owners usually pay yearly maintenance fees, which can rise over time.
The painful part is selling.
Resale prices are often a small fraction of what buyers paid, sometimes close to nothing.
Here is your protection.
Never sign on the day of the presentation. Take the papers home.
Add up the fees for ten years, not just the price.
Check resale listings for the same resort before you decide.
And if you already signed, many states give you a few days to cancel.
Read the contract for that deadline, and act fast.
A free gift is never free if it costs your judgment.
Follow for more tricks hiding behind free offers.

caption: Timeshare presentations explained: the free vacation, the pressure to sign today, the yearly fees, the resale problem, and how to protect yourself.

lines.text: Paper envelopes helped families save more money.
The envelope method is old and simple.
On payday, you split your cash into envelopes.
Groceries. Fun. Gas. Gifts.
When an envelope is empty, that category is done for the month.
It sounds too basic to work. Research says otherwise.
Researchers ran a study with construction workers in rural India.
Their savings went into sealed envelopes.
When the savings were split across two envelopes instead of one, families saved more.
Opening a second envelope felt like a new decision. A small wall.
And when the envelopes had photos of their children on them, it worked even better.
Spending that money suddenly felt like taking it from the kids.
Money with a name and a face is harder to waste.
You do not need cash to use this.
Many banks let you create separate savings pots with names.
Name them for the goal, and add a photo if your app allows it.
Split your money before you can spend it, not after.
Follow for more money habits backed by research.

caption: Why cash envelopes work: a study with workers in rural India found split envelopes and photos of their children helped families save more, and how to copy it.

lines.text: A Coca Cola cost five cents for about seventy years.
From eighteen eighty six until about nineteen fifty nine, a bottle cost one nickel.
Two world wars. The Great Depression. Prices everywhere went up and down.
Coke stayed at five cents.
Not by accident, and not out of kindness.
Economists wrote a whole paper on why.
First, an early contract with the bottlers made raising the price very hard.
Second, vending machines.
Coke machines were built to take a single coin. A nickel.
The next step up was a dime, double the price, too big a jump.
So the price stayed frozen while costs slowly climbed.
Eventually, inflation won, and the nickel Coke disappeared.
There is a lesson here for today.
When companies cannot raise a price, they often change the product instead.
Smaller packs, cheaper ingredients, new fees.
A price that never moves is not always a deal. Check what you get for it.
And remember, a famous low price can be great advertising for everything else.
Follow for more surprising stories from the history of prices.

caption: How Coca Cola stayed at five cents for about seventy years, from eighteen eighty six to nineteen fifty nine, and what froze the price.

lines.text: Candy waits at the checkout because you are waiting too.
The checkout is the one spot every shopper must pass.
You stand still. You are tired. Your kids are bored.
And right at eye level, sweets and snacks.
It works so well that governments stepped in.
Researchers in Britain studied supermarkets that removed sweets from checkouts.
Purchases of small sugary snacks from the checkout dropped by about seventeen percent.
And a year later, they were still about fifteen percent lower.
Those were snacks people never planned to buy.
In twenty twenty two, England went further.
Larger stores can no longer put many unhealthy foods at checkouts, entrances or aisle ends.
In most other places, the candy is still waiting.
Here is how to get through the line.
Pick self checkout or a lane without sweets, if your store has one.
Keep your hands busy. Hold your list, or your phone.
Tell kids before you go in that the checkout is a candy free zone.
Plan for the line, and the line cannot plan for you.
Follow for more tricks waiting at the register.

caption: Why candy waits at the checkout: what British researchers found when supermarkets removed sweets from the line, England's twenty twenty two rules, and how to get through.

lines.text: Percent off or dollars off is a deliberate choice.
Wharton marketing professor Jonah Berger calls it the rule of one hundred.
Under one hundred dollars, a percent looks bigger.
A twenty dollar shirt at twenty five percent off sounds better than five dollars off.
Over one hundred dollars, it flips.
On a two thousand dollar laptop, five hundred dollars off sounds bigger than twenty five percent.
Same discount. Same final price. Different feeling.
Smart stores show you whichever number is bigger.
Your brain reacts to the size of the number, not the size of the saving.
And bigger always feels better.
The same trick shows up in bundles.
Save thirty percent sounds great, until you see you are buying three of something you needed one of.
So translate every deal into one thing.
How much money leaves your account, compared with not buying it at all.
Five dollars off a shirt you did not need is not saving five dollars.
It is spending fifteen.
Unless you were going to buy it anyway.
Follow so the bigger number stops working on you.

caption: The rule of one hundred: why stores show percent off on cheap items and dollars off on expensive ones, and how to translate every deal into real money.

lines.text: Your delivery app meal often costs more before any fees.
Look at the menu prices on the app, then at the restaurant.
They are often not the same.
Reporters ordered the same food in store and on delivery apps from thirteen restaurants.
All but two charged more on the apps, about twenty percent more on average.
An industry analysis found similar premiums, even higher at fast food chains.
Why? Restaurants often pay the apps a commission on every order.
Depending on the plan, that can be up to thirty percent.
So many restaurants raise app prices to cover it.
Then come the delivery fee, the service fee, and the tip.
A ten dollar meal can quietly become twenty.
You pay for convenience in four different places.
Here is how to cut it.
Compare the app price with the restaurant's own menu or website.
Order pickup when you can, and skip the delivery and service fees.
Or call the restaurant directly. Some offer their own delivery.
Convenience is worth paying for. Just know how much you are paying.
Follow for more tricks hiding behind the order button.

caption: Delivery app markups: reporters found most restaurants charged about twenty percent more on apps before any fees, why it happens, and how to cut the cost.

lines.text: Free returns make you buy more than you send back.
It sounds like the store is taking a risk.
If you do not like it, send it back for free.
But researchers combined twenty two studies on return policies.
Easy returns did increase returns. But they increased purchases even more.
A safety net makes it easier to say yes.
And once the item is in your home, it starts to feel like yours.
Sending it back takes effort. Printing, packing, a trip to the drop off.
So a lot of maybe purchases quietly become keeps.
Returns are still huge.
American retailers expected about eight hundred ninety billion dollars in returns in twenty twenty four.
That is almost seventeen percent of sales.
Here is how to use free returns without being used.
Only buy what you would buy with no returns allowed.
Put the return deadline in your calendar the day it arrives.
And decide within two days, while the tags are still on.
Free returns are a promise. Use them, or they use you.

caption: Why free returns make you buy more: a review of twenty two studies found easy returns raise purchases more than returns, and how to use them without being used.

lines.text: One company named its cancel process after an epic war.
Inside Amazon, the Prime cancellation flow had a nickname. Iliad.
Like the ancient poem about the long siege of Troy.
Regulators said it took several pages of offers and warnings to finally cancel.
Signing up, by contrast, could take a click.
In twenty twenty five, Amazon agreed to pay two and a half billion dollars to settle the case.
One billion of it was a civil penalty, the largest the agency had ever won.
Amazon did not admit wrongdoing, but agreed to make cancelling simple.
Designers call it a roach motel. Easy to get in, hard to get out.
Every extra screen is a chance for you to give up.
Wait, do you want fifty percent off for three months?
Are you sure you want to lose your benefits?
Each question is designed to make leaving feel like losing.
Here is how to leave on the first try.
Decide before you start, and say no to every offer you did not plan.
Screenshot the final confirmation and keep the email.
Then check your next statement to make sure the charge is gone.
If leaving takes a maze, staying was never really your choice.
Follow for more tricks that keep your money on a subscription.

caption: Why cancelling is so hard: Amazon's Prime cancel flow nicknamed Iliad, the two and a half billion dollar settlement in twenty twenty five, and how to leave fast.
